newsitem.title: USA: Funds look south of the border.
newsitem.headline: Funds look south of the border.

text.p: Investment analysts lately have been encouraging investors to buy shares of funds that invest in Latin America. But some investors who held shares of the funds back in late 1994 think that's ridiculous advice.
The sceptics remember how Mexico's currency crisis back then caused such funds' share prices to plummet. Some Latin America funds lost 20 percent or more during 1995.

Since then, Latin America funds have staged a comeback, gaining some 26.1 percent on average during 1996 compared with a 19.2 percent return for the typical domestic growth fund. But many investors still are wary of holding these high-risk funds, especially when safer domestic entries are delivering double-digit returns.

In fact, many investors should avoid the funds under any circumstances. Over time, a fund that concentrates its assets in a single overseas region is likely to be extremely volatile -- especially when the region is known for political and economic instability. Thus, most investors are better off investing the bulk of their assets in diversified domestic and international funds.

Those who want to take on the added risk of emerging markets can choose an international fund that invests primarily in developed countries such as Japan or the countries of Western Europe, but leaves room for a modest stake in emerging markets.
An example is the T. Rowe Price International Stock (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load), which recently held around 20 percent of its assets in emerging market stocks.
More adventurous sorts can choose an emerging markets fund that invests in more than one region.

Vanguard International Equity Index Fund Emerging Markets (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum investment; no-load) invests in the Pacific Rim, which recently accounted for 50 percent of its holdings; Latin America (24 percent); Eastern Europe (4 percent) and elsewhere.

Only the boldest investors -- those who can afford to ride out significant losses and hold their shares for at least five years -- should take the risk of concentrating significant sums in a fund that specialises in Latin America.

For those investors, however, analysts point out that now might be a good time to consider investing in such specialised funds. Rapid growth in global trade has increased prosperity in many Latin American countries, and analysts estimate that corporate profits in the region could rise 25 percent this year.

Mark Madden, manager of Pioneer Emerging Markets Fund (800-225-6292; $1,000 minimum investment; 5.75 percent load), points out that the Brazilian economy is opening up to more private investment, while Argentina is emerging from a severe recession. Mexico also is recovering from its recession, he adds. Even the Mexican peso's value has begun to stabilise -- although the notorious volatility of that currency still poses some risks to investors.

Meanwhile, many stocks in Latin American markets are trading at relatively low prices. That's in part because investors have been distracted by the large gains of U.S. stocks and funds that hold them.
In addition, some investors still haven't forgiven Latin American funds for the losses those funds inflicted on many portfolios after the Mexican currency crisis.
Investors who can take even greater risks might consider shares of some so-called closed-end funds that invest in Latin America. Like individual stocks, closed-end funds trade on stock exchanges.

As a result, the funds' share prices fluctuate with investor demand. When a region such as Latin America is out of fashion, shares of closed-end funds that invest there may trade at prices well below the value of the assets in their portfolios--that is, their "net asset values" (NAV).

Recently, a number of closed-end funds that invest in Latin America have traded at significant discounts from their net asset values. Trouble is, they are even more specialised than ordinary funds that invest in the region.
The closed-end offerings tend to pick a single country and invest there -- exposing shareholders to potentially wild swings in share prices.

That said, risk-tolerant investors might consider funds such as Chile Fund, which recently traded on the New York Stock Exchange for $21 a share -- roughly a 15 percent discount to its net asset value. Chile's stock market and economy have been flat during the past year, but an eventual turnaround could deliver sharp gains to patient shareholders.

Another choice for investors who thrive on risk is the Brazil Fund (NYSE; $22; 14.9 percent discount). The fund typically invests in blue-chip Brazilian companies with no debt, experienced management and strong positions in their markets. That can't protect shareholders from the occasional stomach-turning market upset. But it will help them share in the country's economic growth, which is likely to be rapid, if uneven, in the coming decade.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
